Water in, water out

From almost none to a great deal: it depends on the cooling.

How it works
›
none
evaporated a year, at most (dry coolers)
—
make-up water a year (2–6 cycles)
0 m³
rain on the roof a year
about 1,303 m³
water behind its electricity a year (Alberta 2021: 85% coal and gas at ~1.25 L/kWh, 3% hydro at ~16.8; CER profile, to check)

Water hardness sets how often tower water must be bled off: Edmonton's treated water is about 178 mg/L as CaCO₃ (EPCOR, 2026), Vancouver's about 20 (Metro Vancouver, 2025), so the same tower runs fewer cycles and blows down more in Edmonton. more

Conventional: air-cooled, dry coolers, no heat recovery. Modelled Vancouver and Edmonton rows sit on the worked-example lots (1425 Clark Dr; 12603 123 Street Nw). What changes, and when

Pipes and grid connections outlast the servers and the tenants. Each red tick is a point where the heat could change.

0 yr

Servers replaced
every 5–6 years
Colocation contract
2–5 years, renewed or not
Hyperscale contract
5–10+ years
Heat contract (Stockholm)
10 years + 5
Cooling and heat pumps
15–25 years
Building shell
up to about 40 years
Pipe network
30–50 years, by water temperature
Grid connection
stays with the land
Four futures
Tenant changes cooling: liquid to air: heat offered drops to none; air to liquid: heat could be offered
Tenant changes cooling
liquid to air: heat offered drops to none; air to liquid: heat could be offered
Tenant leaves
receivers fall back on their own heating at full peak; the grid connection and pipe stay
Receiver leaves
all heat goes back to the dry coolers, so they must stay full size
Network arrives
a district network reaching the site could take what neighbours cannot
